a: Removes the noise around speech with the DeepFilterNet3 model (DeNoise without it). Voice Isolation keeps speech and removes everything else: fans, traffic, keyboard clicks, wind, room hum. It is a trained neural network, so it handles noise that changes from moment to moment, which a classic noise reducer can't follow.

q: What does Cleaning up a voice by hand do, and how do I use it?
a: The order to fix a voice by hand: rumble, noise, hum, esses, level, tone, loudness. Listen first, on headphones. Note what is wrong: rumble (traffic, handling, a desk), steady noise (fan, hiss), changing noise (traffic, keyboard, wind), hum, harsh "s" sounds, a voice that jumps between quiet and loud. Fix only what you hear. Remove rumble. Reduce Rumble at about 3 (66 Hz); go to 4 (78 Hz) if the low end still booms. A voice has nothing useful below ~70 Hz, so this is safe on almost every voice. Reduce the noise. Compare the noise in the pauses with the voice: - noise you only hear in the pauses (more than ~40 dB under the voice): leave it; - quiet steady noise: Reduce Noise at 3–5; - loud or changing noise: Voice Isolation at 7–10. Listen to the voice itself while you raise it; stop where the voice starts to sound processed. Hum (only if you hear a steady low tone): DeHum at the mains frequency (50 Hz in most of the world, 60 Hz in the Americas).

q: What does Clean Up Voice (one click) do, and how do I use it?
a: One click measures a voice clip and sets the Essential Sound controls and loudness. It does the manual process above for you as a starting point: it measures the clip (noise floor against the voice level, energy below 80 Hz, how sharp the "s" sounds are, how much the level varies; with the Voice Isolation model installed it also lets the model measure how much of the sound is noise, which catches key clicks and wind gusts between words) and sets the same visible controls: Reduce Rumble, Voice Isolation (when its model is installed, else Reduce Noise), DeEss, Dynamics, and Loudness matched to −14 LUFS with the true peak held under −1 dBTP. It is one undo step, and every slider it sets stays yours to change.

q: What does Recording a voice-over do, and how do I use it?
a: Records narration from a microphone onto a track at the playhead, with pre-roll, countdown and punch-in. Pick the microphone and its input channel in Voice-Over Record Settings (`audio.voiceover.settings`), with the file name to use (default "Voice-over"), the countdown beeps (on) and the pre-roll and post-roll (2 seconds each). Park the playhead where the voice should start, or set In and Out to punch in: recording then covers only that range. Click the record button in the audio track's header (`audio.voiceover.start`). Playback starts the pre-roll earlier so you can hear the lead-in; the beeps count down to the record point. Stop (`audio.voiceover.stop`, or reaching the Out point). The recording is written as a mono WAV file (Project Settings ▸ Scratch Disks, else next to the project), imported and placed on the track: one undo step. The pre-roll isn't kept.

q: What does Write a lesson do, and how do I use it?
a: How contributors write a lesson file. `expect` is exactly one of: - `{ command = "id" }` (or a list of up to 8 ids), optionally with `params`: the step is done when that command succeeds with matching parameters. A table in `params` must match the same keys (other keys are ignored); `{ gt = 1.0 }`, `ge`, `lt`, `le`, `ne` compare numbers; `{ any = true }` means "present"; `{ nonzero = true }` means "a number, or a number in a list, other than 0"; `{ in = ["a", "b"] }` means "one of these"; a list matches item by item. Example: `params = { clips = [{ any = true }] }` (at least one clip selected). - `{ element = "automation.id" }`: done when that control is on screen (for "open this tab" steps). - `{ manual = true }`: the reader presses Next. A step may add `already = "clipSelected"`: it finishes by itself when it starts (or on `coach.state`) while a clip on a video track is selected. Use it only where any clip will do, never where the lesson needs a particular clip (a face, a noisy shot, a reference). Use only real command ids and automation ids. The engine test checks every command id; the UI test in `crates/ui-egui/tests/ui/coach_ui.rs` walks each lesson and checks that every outlined control is on screen. Write in your own words, plain language, why before how. Never copy a manual.

q: What does Why do, and how do I use it?
a: Why log footage needs its colour space known and a working space to grade in. A log clip stores brightness with a curve that squeezes the sun and the shadows into a flat picture, and its colours use a gamut (F-Gamut) wider than your screen. Grading numbers only mean the same thing from clip to clip if all clips are first translated into one working space. This fork uses DaVinci Wide Gamut / DaVinci Intermediate (Blackmagic's published specification). Its signal has mid grey at about 0.336, which is why the Pivot slider defaults to that value. Grade nodes work on this signal when the sequence's working space is DaVinci Wide Gamut; in a Rec. 709 sequence they work on the Rec. 709 signal, in a Rec. 2100 sequence on the PQ or HLG signal, so the same numbers look different in each.

q: What does Using the Lumetri Color panel do, and how do I use it?

(In the Color Grading workspace it is a tab beside Primaries.) If the clip has no Lumetri yet, click Add Lumetri Color to clip (the same as `effects.apply` with the effect `lumetri`). Work down the sections, each with an on / off switch: - Basic Correction: Input LUT (`lumetri.setInputLut`), Temperature, Tint, Saturation, Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks (HDR White / HDR Specular in an HDR sequence). - Creative: a Look LUT (`lumetri.setLook`) with Intensity, Faded Film, Sharpen, Vibrance, Saturation. - Curves: RGB curves and the Hue vs Sat / Hue vs Hue / Hue vs Luma / Luma vs Sat / Sat vs Sat curves. - Color Wheels & Match: Shadows / Midtones / Highlights wheels and Color Match. - HSL Secondary: a hue / saturation / luma key with Soften, Denoise and Blur, Show Mask, and a correction for the keyed area. - Vignette: Amount, Midpoint, Roundness, Feather. Auto balance does it from the frame's greys (`lumetri.wb.auto`). It samples the clip as Lumetri's white balance sees it (after the Input LUT), so picking twice gives the same values; clipped (judged on the footage itself, as for the node picker), too dark or too colourful spots are refused with a reason. Unlike the node picker, it removes keyframes from Temperature / Tint (as Apply Match does). Same solver as the node grader's WB picker (primaries.md); in Premiere the selector may weigh the cast differently, so values won't match Premiere's.

q: What does How it works do, and how do I use it?
a: How the spatial (bilateral) and temporal filters decide what is noise. Spatial: an edge-preserving *bilateral* filter: each pixel is averaged with its neighbours, weighted by distance and by how similar they are, so a real edge (a big difference) is left alone while small random differences are averaged out. Brightness (luma) and colour (two colour differences) are filtered separately with their own strengths. The filter size follows the picture size, so a reduced-resolution preview looks like the full-size export.

q: What does How H.265 is encoded, and when it falls back do, and how do I use it?
a: H.265 is encoded by the graphics card's video engine, falling back when it can't. Leave Auto unless you have a reason. Pick Hardware (VA-API) when you'd rather know than wait for a slow software export; pick Software (x265) for archives. After an export, `perf.stats` names the encoder that was actually used. Keep 4:2:0 (delivery) for anything you upload or send to be watched. Pick 4:2:2 (master, 10-bit) for a master you will grade or cut again. It is always 10-bit, so the Profile choice is hidden. FilmCraft picks a video engine that can encode it by itself (here Intel's: the AMD card has none); on a machine without one the export falls back to software x265, which is slow at 6.2K. Many players and phones can't play 4:2:2 HEVC; that is expected for a master.

q: What does HDR sequences export as Main 10 do, and how do I use it?
a: HDR sequences export as 10-bit H.265 Main 10 to avoid banding. a: Pins a picture onto a screen or sign with Corner Pin's Track Surface. Put the shot with the screen on Video 1 and the picture you want on the screen on Video 2, above it, over the same frames. Apply Corner Pin (Effects ▸ Video Effects ▸ Distort) to the clip on Video 2. Go to a frame where the screen is clearly visible. In Effect Controls (the Inspector in the Resolve workflow), set Upper Left, Upper Right, Lower Left and Lower Right to the screen's four corners. The picture now sits on the screen in this frame. On Corner Pin's Track Surface row, click ▶▶ (track forward) or ◀◀ (track backward); the single-arrow buttons track one frame at a time. The track runs in the background, shows its progress in the jobs list, and clicking any of the buttons again stops it. What was tracked before stopping is kept.

q: What does Selecting edit points do, and how do I use it?
a: Selects one or more edit points to trim, nearest to the playhead or by clicking. q: What does Dynamic trimming and playing around the edit do, and how do I use it?
a: Trims while playing with J, K and L, and plays around a selected edit. q: What does Multicam controls do, and how do I use it?
a: The multicam monitor's layout and pages, recording angle cuts, audio follows video, editing the camera list. Make the multicam clip and put it on a sequence (editing.md), then show the multi-camera view in the Program monitor (`multicam.toggleView`). Play and click angles: with recording on (`multicam.recordStart` / `recordStop`) each click becomes a cut; without it, `multicam.cut` / `multicam.switchAngle` change the angle at the playhead. Audio Follows Video (`multicam.audioFollowsVideo`): the sound switches with the picture; off, one angle's sound plays throughout (the usual choice for an interview with one good microphone). With many cameras, choose the grid (`multicam.gridLayout`) and step through pages of angles (`multicam.page`, `nextPage`, `prevPage`). Edit Cameras… (`multicam.editCameras`) renames angles or turns them off. `multicam.autoAdjustQuality` lowers the preview quality so many angles play smoothly.
